n: After finishing his sermon to the people, Jesus went back to Capernaum, his home base.

f.w: in the audience of the people
f.g: In the hearing of the people.

n: A Roman centurion there had a servant he valued highly, who was sick and about to die. This officer cared deeply about someone society considered property.

f.g: A Roman army officer over about 100 soldiers — here likely serving Herod Antipas.
Highly valued, precious to him.

n: Hearing about Jesus, he sent some Jewish elders to ask Jesus to come heal his servant. As a Gentile, he approached respectfully through local leaders.

f.g: Respected leaders of the local Jewish community.

n: The elders pleaded earnestly with Jesus, saying this man deserved his help.

f.g: Earnestly, urgently.

n: He loves our nation and even built our synagogue for us. Here was a Gentile who had blessed God’s people.

f.w: he hath built us a synagogue
f.g: Remains of a later synagogue in Capernaum stand on what may be the foundation of an earlier one.

n: Jesus went with them. Near the house, the centurion sent friends with a message: Lord, don’t trouble yourself — I’m not worthy to have you under my roof. He knew a Jew might become ritually unclean entering a Gentile home.
That’s why I didn’t come to you myself. Just say the word, and my servant will be healed. He believed Jesus’ word alone had power, even at a distance.

f.g: Simply speak the command.

n: He explained: I understand authority. I’m under orders myself, and I have soldiers under me who go and come when I command. He recognized that Jesus held authority over sickness.
Jesus was amazed. He turned to the crowd and said he hadn’t found such great faith even in Israel. Faith can be found in unexpected places.

f.g: Was astonished.

n: When the messengers returned to the house, they found the servant completely healthy.

f.g: Healthy, fully recovered.

n: The next day Jesus went to Nain, a village southwest of the Sea of Galilee, followed by his disciples and a large crowd.

f.g: A village near Mount Tabor, about 6 miles southeast of Nazareth.

n: At the town gate they met a funeral procession. The dead man was his mother’s only son, and she was a widow. Without husband or son, she faced grief and likely poverty. Many townspeople were with her.

f.w: the only son of his mother

n: When the Lord saw her, his heart went out to her, and he said, “Don’t cry.” No one asked him to help; his compassion moved him first.
He stepped forward and touched the open coffin, and the bearers stood still. He said, “Young man, I tell you, get up!”

f.g: An open stretcher or frame used to carry the dead to burial.

n: The dead man sat up and began to talk, and Jesus gave him back to his mother — words echoing Elijah’s miracle for another widow.

f.w: he delivered him to his mother

n: Awe swept over everyone. They praised God, saying a great prophet had appeared among them and God had come to help his people.
The news about him spread throughout Judea and all the surrounding region.

f.g: Report, news (not necessarily untrue).

n: John’s disciples reported all these things to John, who was in prison.

f.g: Told, reported.

n: John sent two of his disciples to ask Jesus: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we look for someone else?” Many think John sent them so his followers could see for themselves.

f.g: A title for the expected Messiah.

n: The two delivered John’s question word for word.
Right then Jesus healed many of illnesses, afflictions, and evil spirits, and gave sight to many blind people.

f.g: Painful afflictions.

n: His answer was to point to the evidence: go tell John what you’ve seen and heard — the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor hear good news. These were Isaiah’s signs of the Messiah.
And blessed is anyone who doesn’t stumble over me — who isn’t put off because I don’t fit their expectations.

f.g: Caused to stumble, to fall away.

n: After the messengers left, Jesus spoke about John: what did you go out to the desert to see? A reed blowing in the wind? John was no flimsy, wavering man.

f.w: A reed shaken with the wind
f.g: Reeds grew along the Jordan; the image suggests someone easily swayed.

n: A man in fancy clothes? People who dress in luxury live in palaces — where John was now a prisoner, not a courtier.

f.g: Live in luxury.

n: A prophet? Yes — and much more than a prophet.
He is the one Malachi wrote about: the messenger sent ahead to prepare the way.

f.w: I send my messenger before thy face

n: No one born of a woman is greater than John. Yet the least in God’s kingdom is greater than he. Joseph Smith taught that the one “least” in the kingdom referred to Jesus himself.

f.w: there is not a greater prophet than John the Baptist

n: The ordinary people and even tax collectors who heard this acknowledged that God’s way was right, since they had been baptized by John.

f.g: Declared God to be right, accepted his plan.

n: But the Pharisees and experts in the law rejected God’s purpose for them by refusing John’s baptism. Rejecting God’s servants means rejecting God’s plan for ourselves.

f.w: rejected the counsel of God against themselves

f.g: Experts in the law of Moses, not courtroom attorneys.

n: Jesus asked: how can I describe the people of this generation? What are they like?

f.g: To what.

n: They’re like children in the marketplace complaining to each other: we played the flute and you wouldn’t dance; we sang a funeral song and you wouldn’t cry. Nothing pleases them.

f.g: Played the flute — as at a wedding.

n: John came fasting and abstaining from wine, and you said he had a demon.

f.w: neither eating bread nor drinking wine

n: The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and you call him a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners. Critics will find fault no matter what.

f.g: Heavy drinker.

f.w: a friend of publicans and sinners
f.g: Meant as an insult, but a beautiful truth about Jesus.

n: But God’s wisdom is proven right by all who follow it. The results in people’s lives show who was wise.

f.w: wisdom is justified of all her children

n: A Pharisee named Simon invited Jesus to dinner. Jesus accepted and reclined at the table. Jesus ate with Pharisees as well as sinners.

f.g: Reclined at the meal, lying on a couch with feet stretched away from the table.

n: A woman in that town known as a sinner learned Jesus was eating there and came with an alabaster jar of perfume. Banquets were semi-public, so onlookers could enter.

f.g: A flask of perfumed oil carved from soft stone.
Probably someone with a publicly known immoral past; Luke doesn’t name her.

n: She stood behind him at his feet, weeping. Her tears fell on his feet; she wiped them with her hair, kissed his feet, and anointed them with the perfume. Her actions poured out repentance and gratitude.

f.w: wipe them with the hairs of her head
f.g: Letting down her hair in public was considered shocking — she cared more about honoring him than her reputation.

n: The host thought to himself: if this man were a prophet, he’d know what kind of woman is touching him — a sinner. He assumed a holy man would avoid her.

f.g: Had invited him.

n: Jesus, reading his thoughts, said, “Simon, I have something to tell you.” “Go ahead, Teacher.” Jesus proved he was a prophet by knowing Simon’s mind.

f.g: Something.

n: A moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii (about a year and a half of wages); the other owed fifty.

f.g: Denarii; one was about a day’s wage.

n: Neither could repay, so he generously canceled both debts. Which one will love him more?

f.g: Freely, graciously.

n: Simon answered, “I suppose the one who was forgiven more.” Jesus said, “You have judged correctly.”
Turning to the woman, Jesus said: Simon, do you see this woman? You didn’t give me water to wash my feet — a basic courtesy — but she washed them with her tears and dried them with her hair.

f.w: thou gavest me no water for my feet
f.g: Hosts normally offered water to wash dusty feet.

n: You didn’t greet me with a kiss, but she hasn’t stopped kissing my feet since I came in.

f.g: A kiss on the cheek was the customary greeting for a guest.

n: You didn’t anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with perfume.

f.w: My head with oil thou didst not anoint

n: So her many sins have been forgiven — her great love shows it. But whoever is forgiven little loves little. Recognizing our need for forgiveness deepens our love for the Savior.

f.g: Her love is the evidence of forgiveness, not the payment for it, as the parable shows.

f.w: Her sins, which are many, are forgiven

n: Then Jesus said to her directly, “Your sins are forgiven.” He spoke the words she most needed to hear.
The other guests began asking among themselves: who is this who even forgives sins?
Jesus told the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.” She left with a new life. Faith in Christ brings forgiveness and peace.
